checks.title: Internal URL returns 4xx
checks.description: This internal URL, a page or a resource such as an image or script, answered with a 4xx client error such as 404 Not Found, 410 Gone or 403 Forbidden.
checks.fix: If the URL should work, restore it or 301-redirect it to the closest replacement. If it's gone for good, keep the 404 or 410 and update or remove the links and sitemap entries that point to it.
checks.why: Visitors who follow a link here get an error instead of the content. Google doesn't index URLs that return 4xx, and drops ones that were already indexed. A 404 or 410 is the right answer for something removed on purpose, and a 401 or 403 is normal behind a login: then the only problem is the links and sitemap entries that still lead here.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Pages or files that can't be found
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site answer with an error instead of a page or file, most often "not found" (a 404).
Visitors who follow a link to one get an error page, and Google drops addresses like these from its results.
That's the right answer for something you removed on purpose, as long as nothing still links to it.
plainFix: Look at each address in the list and decide whether it should still exist.
If it should, put the page or file back.
If it has moved, forward the old address to the new one (a "301 redirect"), in your site's redirect settings or through your developer.
If it's gone for good, leave it, and remove the links that still point to it.
checks.plainPassed: No page or file answers with a "not found" error

checks.title: Internal URL returns 5xx
checks.description: The server answered this internal URL with a 5xx error, such as 500 Internal Server Error or 503 Service Unavailable. Temporary errors (502, 503 and 504) were retried before being recorded.
checks.fix: Check the server and application logs for this URL at the time of the crawl, fix the cause and recrawl. If many URLs failed together, the server may have been overloaded: recrawl at a slower speed preset to see whether the errors stop.
checks.why: Visitors get an error page instead of the content. Google slows down crawling when a site returns 5xx errors, and URLs that keep failing are eventually dropped from its index. A one-off error during a busy crawl can happen, so recheck the URL; errors that repeat or hit many URLs need fixing first.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Pages or files that fail with a server error
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site answer with a server error, such as "internal server error" (a 500).
Visitors see an error page, and Google visits a site less often while the errors go on.
One error on a busy day can be a blip, but errors that repeat mean something on the server is broken.
plainFix: Open two or three of the addresses in your browser to see whether they still fail.
If they do, send the list to your developer or hosting company: the cause will be in the server's error log.
If they load now, check the site again at the "Polite" speed: the check itself may have been too much for the server.
checks.plainPassed: No page or file fails with a server error

checks.title: Internal URL didn't respond
checks.description: This internal URL gave no response: the request timed out (after 20 seconds by default) or the connection failed, even after retries (2 by default). Both can be changed in the crawl settings.
checks.fix: Check whether the URL loads from another network, then look for dropped or slow connections at the server, firewall, load balancer or DNS. If it only fails under load, the server needs more capacity or caching; a slower speed preset shows whether the crawl itself caused it.
checks.why: Visitors get a browser error or a page that never loads. Google treats timeouts, connection resets and DNS errors like server errors: it slows crawling straight away, can't index URLs it gets nothing from, and removes indexed ones within days if the problem continues.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Pages or files that don't answer
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site gave no answer at all: the connection failed, or the wait ran out.
Visitors get a browser error or a page that never loads, and Google can't list an address it gets nothing from.
It can also happen when the check itself asks faster than the server can cope with.
plainFix: Open two or three of the addresses in your browser to see whether they load for you.
If they don't, send the list to your developer or hosting company and ask what is dropping or delaying connections.
If they do, check the site again at the "Polite" speed to see whether the check was too much for the server.
checks.plainPassed: No page or file failed to answer

checks.title: Internal URL blocked by a firewall
checks.description: A firewall, bot protection service (such as Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS WAF, DataDome or Imperva) or a rate limit (HTTP 429) refused the crawler on this internal URL. The detail names the protection when it's recognised.
checks.fix: Allowlist the crawler in the firewall or bot protection (by user agent, IP address or a secret header), or crawl at a slower speed preset. Make sure the same rules let verified search engine crawlers through: verify Googlebot by reverse DNS or Google's published IP ranges rather than by user agent, which anyone can fake.
checks.why: Nothing on this URL could be checked, so other checks can't see its problems. If the same rules challenge search engine crawlers, they can't crawl it either, and Google slows its crawling of sites that answer with 429. Many protections only challenge automated traffic, so visitors are usually unaffected.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Pages or files your site's security wouldn't show
plainWhat: Your site's firewall or security service turned the check away from some addresses, so they couldn't be read.
Any problems on those addresses are missing from these results.
Visitors rarely notice, but if search engines are turned away too, they can't list those addresses.
plainFix: Open one of the addresses in your browser to see that it loads for you.
Ask your hosting company, or whoever runs the firewall, to let Shouting Iguana through, then check the site again.
Ask them to make sure Google and other search engines aren't turned away by the same rules.
Check again at the "Polite" speed if the list shows "too many requests" (a 429): the check was asking too fast.
checks.plainPassed: No page or file was refused by the site's security

checks.title: Soft 404
checks.description: This indexable page returns 200 OK, but its title or H1 reads like an error message (such as "Page not found" or "no longer available") and it has fewer than 300 words.
checks.fix: Return 404 or 410 for content that's gone, or 301-redirect it to a real replacement. If the page should exist, change the wording that makes it look like an error, and check its content didn't fail to load.
checks.why: Google detects pages like this as soft 404s and excludes them from search, but keeps crawling them, which wastes crawling on large sites. Serving an error with 200 also hides real breakage from monitoring that only looks at status codes. If the page is fine and only mentions "not found" in a heading, ignore this.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that read like an error page
plainWhat: These pages have a title or main heading that reads like an error message, such as "Page not found", and little text.
Yet they tell search engines they loaded normally, so Google keeps coming back to pages it won't show (it calls them "soft 404s").
If a page is real and its heading only mentions "not found", there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open each page in the list and see whether it's a real page or an error message.
If it's a real page, change the title or heading so it doesn't read like an error.
If it's an error message, ask your developer to make the address answer "not found" (a 404), or forward it to a replacement.
checks.plainPassed: No page reads like an error page

checks.title: Redirect chain
checks.description: This internal URL (linked from a crawled page, listed in a sitemap or the start URL) takes two or more redirects to reach its final URL. The detail gives the number of hops, and says when there are more than Googlebot follows.
checks.fix: Point each redirect straight at the final URL, and update links and sitemap entries to the final URL so they skip the redirects altogether.
checks.why: Every hop is another round trip before the page starts to load, which visitors on slow connections notice. Google follows up to 10 hops and processes only the final URL's content, and its crawl budget guide says long chains have a negative effect on crawling, which matters mainly on large sites. Two hops is rarely a problem in itself, but chains grow with each site change.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Addresses that forward more than once
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site forward visitors on two or more times before they reach the final address.
Each extra step is a wait before the page starts to load, and Google gives up after 10 steps.
Two steps do little harm, but the steps pile up each time the site changes.
plainFix: Change the links on your pages, and the addresses in your sitemap, to the final address: the list shows it.
Ask your developer or hosting company to forward each old address straight to the final one, in one step (a "301 redirect").
checks.plainPassed: No address forwards more than once

checks.title: Redirect loop
checks.description: Following this internal URL's redirects leads back to a URL already passed, so they never reach a page.
checks.fix: Follow the hops, find the rule that sends the URL back, and change it so the chain ends at a URL that returns 200.
checks.why: Browsers give up with an error (Chrome's ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS), so visitors never see the content and search engines have nothing to index. Loops usually come from two rules undoing each other, such as one adding a trailing slash and another removing it, or an HTTPS redirect on a server behind a CDN or proxy that can't see the visitor is already on HTTPS. Fix this first.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Addresses that forward in a circle
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site forward visitors round in a circle, so they never reach a page.
The browser gives up and shows an error such as "too many redirects", and search engines have nothing to list.
The usual cause is two forwarding rules that undo each other, such as one adding a slash to an address and one removing it.
plainFix: Open one of the addresses in your browser to see the error for yourself.
Send the list to your developer or hosting company and ask them to find the two forwarding rules that undo each other.
Ask them to make each address end at a page that loads, then check the site again.
checks.plainPassed: No address forwards in a circle

checks.title: Broken redirect
checks.description: This internal URL redirects, but the redirects end at a URL that returns a 4xx or 5xx error or doesn't respond, or the redirect has no usable Location header.
checks.fix: Point the redirect at a working replacement or fix the target. If there's no replacement, let the old URL return 404 or 410 rather than redirect to an error.
checks.why: Visitors land on an error instead of the page the redirect promised. Google ignores a redirecting URL's own content and processes only the final URL's, so there's nothing to index, and links to the old URL lead nowhere.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Addresses that forward to a dead end
plainWhat: Some addresses on your site forward visitors on, but to an address that doesn't work, or to nowhere at all.
Visitors land on an error instead of the page they were promised, and search engines find nothing to list.
Every link to the old address, on your site and on others, leads to that error.
plainFix: Look at where each address in the list ends up, and decide which working page should replace it.
Change the forwarding (the "redirect") to point at that page, in your site's redirect settings or through your developer.
If nothing replaces it, remove the forwarding so the old address answers "not found" (a 404), then remove the links to it.
checks.plainPassed: No address forwards to a dead end

checks.title: Temporary redirect
checks.description: This internal URL redirects to another URL on the site with a temporary status code: 302, 303 or 307. Temporary redirects to other sites, such as a shop's hosted login or checkout, don't count: they hand visitors over rather than move the page.
checks.fix: If the move is permanent, change the redirect to 301 or 308; if it's temporary, leave it.
checks.why: Google doesn't treat a temporary redirect as a sign that the target should replace the old URL (at most it's a weak signal), so the old URL can stay in search results. That's correct when the move really is temporary, such as a short-term campaign page or a login redirect. For a permanent move it delays the switch to the new URL.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Forwarding marked as temporary
plainWhat: Some addresses forward visitors to another of your pages with a signal that the move is only temporary.
Google may then keep the old address in its results, which delays the switch when the move is really for good.
That's right for a short-term move, such as a sale page, and then there's nothing to do.
Forwarding to another website, such as a hosted checkout, isn't listed.
plainFix: Look at each address in the list and decide whether its move is for good.
If it's temporary, leave it.
If it's for good, ask your developer or hosting company to change it from temporary (a "302 redirect") to permanent (a "301 redirect").
checks.plainPassed: No forwarding is marked as temporary

checks.title: Redirect from HTTPS to HTTP
checks.description: This internal HTTPS URL redirects to an HTTP URL.
checks.fix: Redirect to the HTTPS version of the target. The cause is usually an old rule or a proxy that rewrites the scheme, so check the server and CDN redirect rules.
checks.why: Visitors who started on a secure URL end on an insecure one that browsers label "Not secure". Google normally prefers HTTPS URLs as canonical, but says HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects make it prefer the HTTP version very strongly, which even HSTS can't override.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Secure addresses that forward to an insecure one
plainWhat: Some secure addresses on your site (starting "https") forward visitors to an insecure one (starting "http").
Browsers label the page they land on "Not secure", and Google is then likely to list the insecure address.
The usual cause is an old forwarding rule that was never updated.
plainFix: Open one of the addresses in your browser and look for "Not secure" beside the address it ends on.
Send the list to your developer or hosting company and ask them to forward each one to the "https" version of where it goes.
Check the site again once it's changed.
checks.plainPassed: No secure address forwards to an insecure one

checks.title: Meta refresh
checks.description: The page has a <meta http-equiv="refresh"> tag that sends visitors to another URL or reloads the page, at once or after a delay. The detail gives the target and the delay.
checks.fix: Replace it with a 301 redirect on the server (or 302 if the move is temporary). If the page reloads itself to show new content, update it with script instead, or let visitors refresh.
checks.why: Google treats an instant meta refresh as a permanent redirect and a delayed one as temporary, but recommends a server-side redirect wherever you can set one up; that's faster too, as the browser doesn't load the page first. A timed redirect or reload also moves content away while people are reading, which WCAG counts as a failure. A refresh on old URLs where the server can't redirect is an acceptable fallback.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that move on or reload by themselves
plainWhat: These pages send visitors to another address, or reload, by themselves: at once, or after a set time.
A timed move takes the page away while people are still reading.
It's also slower than forwarding done by the server, which is what Google recommends.
It's an acceptable fallback only where the server can't forward.
plainFix: Open one of the pages and watch what happens: the list shows where each one sends visitors, and when.
Ask your developer to replace it (it's called a "meta refresh") with forwarding done by the server (a "301 redirect").
If a page reloads to show fresh content, ask for it to update in place instead, or leave visitors to reload.
checks.plainPassed: No page moves on or reloads by itself
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one line in your page design, which every page shares.

checks.title: Links to broken internal URLs
checks.description: The page links to internal URLs that return a 4xx or 5xx error or don't respond, directly or at the end of their redirects (or whose redirects loop). The detail counts them and says where the first goes wrong.
checks.fix: Update each link to the working URL, remove it, or restore the target. For a target that moved, link to its new address rather than to a redirect.
checks.why: Visitors who click hit an error, and search engines spend crawls on URLs they won't index, as Google doesn't index URLs that return 4xx. Links in a template, such as the menu or footer, repeat on every page, so fix those first.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Links that lead to broken pages
plainWhat: Some of your pages have links that lead to an address on your site that doesn't work.
Visitors who click one land on an error page, and search engines waste their visit on it.
A link in a menu or footer repeats on every page, so one bad link can show up hundreds of times.
plainFix: Open each page in the list in your site's editor and find the link.
Point it at the right page, or remove it.
If the same link is on most pages, it's in your menu, footer or page design: fix it there once.
checks.plainPassed: Every link between your pages leads to a working page

checks.title: Links to broken external URLs
checks.description: The page links to URLs on other sites that return a 4xx or 5xx error or don't respond, directly or after redirects. Statuses many sites send only to crawlers (401, 403, 405, 429, 503 and LinkedIn's 999) don't count, and nor do links that the other site's bot protection (such as Cloudflare) refused, or that its robots.txt kept the crawler from checking.
checks.fix: Update each link to the resource's current address or an archived copy, or remove it.
checks.why: Visitors who click hit a dead end, which makes the page look neglected and its references unreliable. Google doesn't document broken outbound links as a ranking factor, so this is about visitors. Some sites refuse crawlers in other ways, so open a few in a browser before editing.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Links to other websites that don't work
plainWhat: Some of your pages link to an address on another website that doesn't work.
Visitors who click one reach a dead end, which makes your page look out of date.
Some websites turn away automatic checks but work for people, so try a link yourself before you change it.
Links that another website's security or rules file kept the check from opening aren't counted.
plainFix: Click a few of the links in your browser to confirm they're really broken.
Open each page in your site's editor and point the link at the new address, if the page has moved.
Remove the link, or swap it for another source, if the page has gone for good.
checks.plainPassed: No link to another website was found broken
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a link in your menu, footer or page design, which every page shares.

checks.title: Links to internal redirects
checks.description: The page links to internal URLs that redirect permanently (301 or 308, or an instant meta refresh) to a working page. Links to temporary redirects (302, 303 or 307), such as a sign-in link that sends visitors on to a login page, don't count: the linked URL is still the one to use.
checks.fix: Change the links to point straight at the final URL. Keep the redirects for bookmarks and other sites' links.
checks.why: Each click costs visitors an extra round trip before the page starts to load, and each crawl costs search engines an extra request. Google's advice is to link to the canonical URL within your site, which a redirecting URL isn't. A few are harmless; it's worth fixing in templates, where the same link repeats on every page.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Links that go through a forwarding address
plainWhat: Some links on your pages point at an address on your site that forwards visitors on for good.
The link still works, but each click takes an extra step, as does each search engine visit.
A few do no harm, so there's nothing to do unless the link is in a menu or footer on every page.
Forwarding that's only for now, such as a sign-in link's, isn't listed.
plainFix: Open a page from the list in your site's editor and find the link: the list shows the address it points at.
Change the link to the address it ends up at.
Leave the forwarding itself in place, for bookmarks and for links from other websites.
checks.plainPassed: No link between your pages goes through a forwarding address
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a link in your menu, footer or page design, which every page shares.

checks.title: Nofollow internal links
checks.description: The page has rel="nofollow" on links to the site's own pages. Links to resources, such as images opened in a gallery lightbox, don't count.
checks.fix: Remove rel="nofollow" from internal links. Block URLs that shouldn't be crawled in robots.txt, or add noindex (without a robots.txt block) to pages that shouldn't appear in search.
checks.why: Google treats nofollow as a hint not to crawl the target through that link or use the link for ranking, so pages linked only this way may be found late or not at all. For links within your own site, Google's advice is to use robots.txt to keep URLs from being crawled, and noindex to keep pages out of search, instead of nofollow. Nofollow on login or basket links is common and mostly harmless, but achieves little.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Links that search engines are told not to follow
plainWhat: Some links between your own pages carry a note that tells search engines not to follow them.
Pages reached only through links like these (marked "nofollow") may be found late by search engines, or not at all.
It's common on login and basket links, where it does little harm and little good.
plainFix: Open a page from the list in your site's editor and find the link: the list shows where it leads.
Remove the "nofollow" setting from the link, often a tick box in the link's options.
If the link is in your menu, footer or page design, ask your developer to take the setting off there, once.
If the aim was to keep a page out of search results, ask your developer to set that on the page itself (a "noindex" setting).
checks.plainPassed: No link between your pages is marked not to be followed
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a link in your menu, footer or page design, which every page shares.

checks.title: Internal links without anchor text
checks.description: The page has internal links with nothing to read: no text, no alt text on an image inside, and no aria-label, aria-labelledby or title. A link to the page itself counts too, as a logo on the home page is; links written as a fragment (#, #top) and links in the <head>, such as rel="amphtml", don't.
checks.fix: Add visible text, alt text on the image inside the link, or an aria-label on icon links. For a logo that links home, alt text with the site name is enough.
checks.why: Screen readers announce these as just "link" or read out the URL, so their users can't tell where they go. Google uses anchor text to understand the page a link points to, and the alt text of a linked image as its anchor text, so an empty link tells it nothing. Icon-only links in a template, such as a logo, a basket or a search icon, usually account for most of them.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Links with nothing to read
plainWhat: Some links on your pages have no words: usually an image or icon, such as a logo, with no description.
People who use a screen reader hear only "link", and search engines learn nothing about the page it leads to.
A logo or icon in the page design is the usual cause, so one fix often clears every page.
Pages are still found either way, so it can wait.
plainFix: Find the link on one of the pages: the list shows where it leads.
If it's an image, give the image a short description (its "alt text"), such as your site's name for a logo.
If it's an icon, ask your developer to add a label to the link (an "aria-label").
checks.plainPassed: Every link between your pages has words to read
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly your logo, which sits in the part of the site every page shares.

checks.title: Links to missing page sections
checks.description: The page links to a #fragment, on itself or another crawled page, that matches no id or named anchor on the target page. App routes (#/, #!), app state (fragments with =, : or &) and #top aren't checked.
checks.fix: Correct the fragment in the link, or add the matching id to the section on the target page; ids on headings are often lost when content is edited or regenerated.
checks.why: Visitors land at the top of the page instead of the section the link promised. Google generally ignores URL fragments, so this is about visitors only. Ids added by JavaScript after the page loads can make a working link look broken, so check it in a browser first.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Links to a part of a page that isn't there
plainWhat: Some links point to a part of a page, such as a heading further down, but that part can't be found.
Visitors land at the top of the page instead of the section the link promised.
Search engines still follow the link to the page, so only visitors are affected.
Some pages build their sections after loading, so if a link works in your browser there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Click the link on one of the pages and see whether it jumps to the right section.
If it doesn't, compare the part of the link after the "#" with the name the section was given (its "anchor" or "id").
Make the two match exactly in your site's editor, or ask your developer to put the name back on the section.
checks.plainPassed: No link points to a missing part of a page
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a link in your page design, such as "Skip to content", which every page shares.

checks.title: Orphan page in a sitemap
checks.description: This indexable page is listed in a sitemap, but no crawled page links to it, not even with a nofollow link or through a redirect. It's only checked when the crawl finished, and not when 1 in 20 or more of the pages it tried to read refused the crawler or didn't answer, as their links are unknown.
checks.fix: If the page matters, link to it from relevant pages and from its section's listing. If it doesn't, remove it from the sitemap, then redirect or remove the page.
checks.why: Visitors can't reach it by browsing, and search engines only know it from the sitemap. Google uses links to find pages and judge their relevance, and says every page you care about should have a link from at least one other page on your site. Often it's an old page left in the sitemap, or one linked only from places a crawler can't follow, such as forms or scripts.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages in your sitemap that nothing links to
plainWhat: No page on your site links to these pages: they were found only in your sitemap.
Visitors can't reach them by browsing, and Google relies on links to find pages and judge what they're about.
They're often old pages left in the sitemap (the file that lists your pages for search engines), or pages reached only through a form.
plainFix: Decide, for each page, whether you still want it.
If you do, link to it from a page where it belongs, such as its category.
If you don't, remove it from the site and from the sitemap.
checks.plainPassed: No page in the sitemap is left with no links to it

checks.title: Noindex page
checks.description: The page has a noindex (or none) directive in a robots meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag header, which asks search engines to keep it out of their results.
checks.fix: Check that it's intended. If the page should appear in search, remove the noindex from the meta tag or header, and make sure robots.txt doesn't block the URL, so search engines can see the change.
checks.why: Google drops a noindex page from its results entirely, even if other sites link to it. That's right for thank-you pages, internal search results, account pages and staging copies. On a page that should rank, a leftover noindex from a launch or a plugin setting is a common reason it vanishes from search.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages told to stay out of search results
plainWhat: These pages carry an instruction that tells search engines to keep them out of search results.
Google drops such a page from its results completely (the instruction is called "noindex").
That's right for thank-you, account and site-search pages, and then there's nothing to do.
It's a problem only on a page you want people to find, where it's often left over from when the site was built.
plainFix: Look down the list for any page you want people to find in search.
Open that page in your site's editor and find a setting such as "Hide this page from search engines", often under "SEO".
Turn the setting off, or ask your developer to remove the "noindex" from the page.
checks.plainPassed: No page is told to stay out of search results

checks.title: Nofollow page
checks.description: The page has a nofollow (or none) directive in a robots meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag header, which asks search engines not to follow any of its links.
checks.fix: Remove nofollow from the robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag header. To qualify individual links to other sites, use rel="nofollow", "sponsored" or "ugc" on those links instead.
checks.why: Search engines that honour it won't use the page's links to discover the pages they point to, so pages linked only from here may go unfound. A page-wide nofollow is rarely intended on a normal page; it's usually left over from a staging setup or set by a plugin.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that tell search engines not to follow their links
plainWhat: These pages tell search engines not to follow any of the links on them.
Pages that are linked only from here may never be found by search engines.
That's rarely meant: it's usually left over from when the site was built, or set by a plugin.
plainFix: Open one of the pages in your site's editor and find a setting about following links, often under "SEO" or "Advanced".
Set it to follow links, or ask your developer to remove the "nofollow" setting from the page.
If only one or two links shouldn't be followed, ask your developer to mark those links instead of the whole page.
checks.plainPassed: No page tells search engines not to follow its links

checks.title: Blocked by robots.txt
checks.description: The crawler didn't fetch this internal URL, because robots.txt disallows it, or because robots.txt itself couldn't be read, which crawlers treat as disallowing everything: the detail then says so. Not checked on a crawl that was told to ignore robots.txt.
checks.fix: If the URL should be crawled, change or remove the Disallow rule that matches it. If it's meant to be blocked, avoid linking to it from crawlable pages where you can, and if it must stay out of search, allow crawling and use noindex instead.
checks.why: Search engines that obey robots.txt can't read the page, so its content, links and any noindex on it go unseen, yet Google can still index the URL without its content, with no description, if links point to it. Blocking is right for URLs with no search value, such as baskets, internal search or filter combinations. It's a problem when a broad rule catches pages you want in search, or the CSS and JavaScript that pages need to render.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Addresses that search engines are told not to visit
plainWhat: Your site's rules file for search engines puts these addresses off limits, so the check didn't read them.
Search engines can't see what's on them, though Google may still list the bare address if other pages link to it.
That's right for baskets and site searches, and then there's nothing to do.
It's a problem if the rule catches pages you want found.
plainFix: Look down the list for any page you want people to find, and for files ending in .css or .js, which pages need to display.
If there are none, leave the rules as they are.
If there are, ask your developer to change the rule that covers them in the rules file (its "robots.txt").
If the list says the rules file couldn't be read, fix that first: it's listed as a problem of its own.
checks.plainPassed: No address is off limits to search engines

checks.title: Search snippet disabled
checks.description: This indexable page has a nosnippet or max-snippet:0 directive in a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag header.
checks.fix: Remove the directive if it isn't intended. To keep only part of the page out of snippets, use the data-nosnippet attribute on that part, or a max-snippet length instead of 0.
checks.why: Google shows the page in results without a text snippet or video preview, and doesn't use its content as direct input for AI Overviews or AI Mode. That can be intended, for example for sensitive content, but a result with no description tells searchers less about the page.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages set to show no text in search results
plainWhat: These pages tell search engines to show no text from the page under its title in search results.
The result is a bare title and address, which tells searchers less, and Google won't quote the page in its AI answers.
That can be deliberate, for private or paid-for content, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Search Google for one of the pages and see whether its result shows any text under the title.
Decide whether you meant these pages to appear that way.
If not, ask your developer to remove the setting the list names, such as "nosnippet", from the pages.
checks.plainPassed: No page blocks its text from search results
checks.plainOneFix: These pages most likely get it from one setting, in your page design or SEO plugin.

checks.title: robots.txt unavailable
checks.description: robots.txt on the site's main origin (the start URL's, or the home page's after redirects) returned a 5xx error or 429, or didn't respond. Reported once, on the home page. Not checked on a crawl told to ignore robots.txt that never read it.
checks.fix: Make /robots.txt answer quickly with 200 and your rules, or with 404 if you don't need any. Check that the firewall, CDN or rate limiting doesn't treat requests for it differently from pages.
checks.why: Google treats a robots.txt it can't fetch as a server error: it stops crawling the whole site for the first 12 hours, then uses its last good copy for up to 30 days (or assumes no restrictions if it has none). If it's still failing after that and the site is otherwise up, Google acts as if there were no robots.txt. Until it's fixed, new and changed pages aren't crawled, so fix this first.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Search engines can't read your site's rules file
plainWhat: The file that tells search engines where they may go on your site (its "robots.txt") answers with an error.
Google stops visiting the whole site when that happens, so new and changed pages don't reach search results.
This is one fault for the whole site, and the first thing to fix.
plainFix: Open your site's address followed by /robots.txt in a browser, to see whether it loads for you.
Send this to your developer or hosting company today: the file must answer normally, or with "not found" if you don't need one.
Ask them to make sure the firewall or security service isn't turning away requests for it.
Check the site again once it's fixed.
checks.plainPassed: The rules file for search engines isn't returning an error
checks.plainLooksFor: A rules file that search engines can't read

checks.title: robots.txt unavailable on another of the site's origins
checks.description: robots.txt on another of the site's origins, such as a subdomain or the http:// version, returned a 5xx error or 429, or didn't respond; the detail names the origin. Origins reached only by the crawler's own probe of the site's other versions aren't included. Not checked on a crawl told to ignore robots.txt, which doesn't read it there.
checks.fix: Make robots.txt on that origin return 200, or 404 if it needs no rules. If the origin shouldn't exist, stop linking to it.
checks.why: Each origin (scheme, host and port) has its own robots.txt, so only that origin is affected: Google stops crawling it for 12 hours, then relies on its last good copy for up to 30 days. The main site carries on as normal. It matters if pages or files you want in search live there, or if that origin's redirects to the main site haven't been picked up yet.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: The rules file on another part of your site can't be read
plainWhat: The rules file for search engines answers with an error on another part of your site, such as shop.example.com.
Google stops visiting that part of the site when that happens, while your main site carries on as normal.
It matters only if that part holds pages or files you want people to find.
plainFix: Open the address the list names in your browser, to see whether the file loads for you.
Send it to your developer or hosting company: the file (a "robots.txt") must answer normally, or with "not found" if it isn't needed.
If that part of the site shouldn't exist, remove the links to it.
checks.plainPassed: No other part of the site has a rules file that fails
checks.plainLooksFor: A rules file that fails on another part of your site

checks.title: robots.txt missing or refused
checks.description: robots.txt returned a 4xx error other than 429 (usually 404, sometimes 401 or 403 from a firewall), or redirected too many times, on the main origin or another of the site's origins. Reported on the home page; the detail lists the origins. A crawl told to ignore robots.txt judges the start URL's origin alone, and not at all when it never read robots.txt.
checks.fix: Add a robots.txt at the origin's root, even if it only holds a Sitemap: line with your XML sitemap's full URL. If a firewall answers it with 401 or 403, let it through.
checks.why: Crawling isn't affected: Google treats a missing robots.txt as having no restrictions, so everything can be crawled. What's missing is a Sitemap: line, which Google, Bing and other search engines read to find your sitemaps, and a way to keep crawlers out of URLs with no search value should you need one. A 401 or 403 meant to keep crawlers out has the opposite effect.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: A rules file for search engines is missing
plainWhat: Search engines that ask for your site's rules file (a "robots.txt") get "not found", or are refused.
They take that to mean they may visit everything, so nothing is held back.
What you miss is a place to tell them where your sitemap is, and to keep them out of pages such as baskets.
If you need neither, there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the address the list names in a browser, to see what answers.
Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin for a "robots.txt" option: most can create the file.
Ask your developer to add one that names your sitemap, if your site has no such option.
Ask your hosting company to let requests for the file through, if a firewall is refusing them.
checks.plainPassed: The site isn't missing its rules file for search engines
checks.plainLooksFor: A missing rules file for search engines

checks.title: Most pages hidden from search
checks.description: The home page is noindex, and so are more than half of the site's pages, so most of the site can't appear in search results. The home page is the page the start URL leads to, after its redirects; while it can be indexed, nothing is reported, however many other pages are noindex. The detail gives the numbers, as in "212 of 240 pages are noindex": the noindex pages, out of the pages the crawl read less the canonicalised ones. A canonicalised page (one that isn't noindex and whose canonical names another URL) is a variant of the page it names, so it isn't in the total. A canonical that leads back to the page, to a broken URL, or to the same page on another version of the site (www or not, http or https) doesn't make a variant. Not checked on a crawl that didn't start at the site's root. Reported once, on the home page.
checks.fix: Find what sets noindex on every page: a "discourage search engines" setting or a staging configuration left on, a robots meta tag in the template, or an X-Robots-Tag header from the server or CDN. Remove it from the pages that should appear in search, then crawl again.
checks.why: Google drops a noindex page from its results, so most of this site can't be found in search. It's nearly always a launch mistake: a staging site's noindex or a "discourage search engines" setting left on. If the pages are meant to stay out, as on a private site or a staging copy, check the noindex pages and ignore this.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Your site hides most of its pages from search
plainWhat: Your home page and more than half of your pages tell search engines to keep them out of search results.
Those pages can't be found through Google, however good they are.
It's often one setting left on from when the site was being built, so one change may fix it.
This is one fault for the whole site, and the first thing to fix.
plainFix: Look in your site's settings for an option such as "Discourage search engines" or "Hide site from search", and turn it off.
If there's no such option, send this to your developer: the list says how many pages are hidden, and how.
Ask them to remove the "noindex" setting.
Check the site again once it's changed.
checks.plainPassed: The site as a whole isn't hidden from search
checks.plainLooksFor: A site that hides its home page and most pages from search

checks.title: Canonicalised page
checks.description: The page's canonical (in the <head> or an HTTP Link header) names a different URL, so the page asks to be treated as a duplicate of it. Canonicals that lead back to this page or to a broken URL don't count.
checks.fix: Check the canonical is intended. If this page should rank, make its canonical point to itself; if it's a true duplicate, link to the canonical URL rather than this one within the site.
checks.why: Google treats a canonical as a strong hint, not a rule: it usually indexes the named URL and folds this page's signals into it, but can choose differently if other signals disagree. That's right for parameter, sorting and print versions of a page. It's a problem when the page has its own content and should rank, as when a template points every canonical at the home page or the first page of a series.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that name another page as the main version
plainWhat: These pages tell search engines that another page is the main version of them (a "canonical" link).
Google then shows that other page instead, which is right for true copies, such as a sorted list or a print version.
It's a problem when the page has its own content, as page 2 of a list does: each page of a list should name itself.
plainFix: Look at each page and the page it points to, and decide whether they're really the same thing.
If they are, there's nothing to do.
If this page should appear in search on its own, ask your developer to point its canonical link at its own address.
checks.plainPassed: No page names another page as the main version

checks.title: Missing canonical
checks.description: This indexable page has no canonical, neither a <link rel="canonical"> in the <head> nor an HTTP Link header.
checks.fix: Add <link rel="canonical" href="..."> to the <head> with the page's own absolute URL; most CMSs and SEO plugins can do this for every page.
checks.why: Google doesn't require one: without it, Google picks the best URL itself when the same content is reachable at several addresses, such as with tracking parameters or with and without a trailing slash. A canonical pointing to the page itself makes your preference explicit, and Google recommends one on canonical pages. Low priority on its own, but it helps most on sites with many URL variants.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that don't name their main address
plainWhat: These pages don't say which address is their main one (they have no "canonical" link).
The same page can often be reached at several addresses, and without this Google picks one itself.
Google usually picks well, so there's nothing to do unless each page can be reached at many addresses.
plainFix: See whether your site's SEO settings or plugin can add a canonical link to every page: most can.
If not, ask your developer to add one to the page design, pointing each page at its own address.
checks.plainPassed: Every page names its main address

checks.title: Conflicting canonicals
checks.description: The page declares two or more different canonical URLs, in the <head>, the HTTP Link header, or across both.
checks.fix: Keep one canonical: find which plugin, theme or server rule adds each and turn off the wrong one. A Link header usually comes from the server, CDN or CMS, not the template.
checks.why: Google has said that when a page specifies more than one canonical, it will likely ignore all of them, so the page effectively has none and Google chooses on its own. It usually comes from two systems, such as a theme and an SEO plugin, or the HTML and a server or CDN header, each adding its own.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that name more than one main address
plainWhat: These pages name two or more different addresses as their main one (they have conflicting "canonical" links).
Google is likely to ignore them all and choose the main address itself.
It usually means two parts of your site each add one, such as the page design and an SEO plugin.
plainFix: Check whether your site has two SEO plugins, or a page design with SEO settings of its own, both switched on.
Turn one of them off, so each page names a single main address.
If you can't find a second source, ask your developer what else adds a canonical link: it can also come from the server.
checks.plainPassed: No page names more than one main address

checks.title: Canonical points to a broken URL
checks.description: The page's canonical names a URL that returns a 4xx or 5xx error or doesn't respond, directly or at the end of its redirects (or its redirects loop).
checks.fix: Point the canonical at the working URL you want indexed, usually this page's own URL, and check templates that build canonicals from a hard-coded host or path.
checks.why: A canonical has to name a working page: Google's own checklist is to make sure the target exists and isn't an error or soft 404. One that leads to an error can't take this page's place, so expect search engines to disregard it and judge this page on its own. The cause is usually a stale URL, such as a staging host, an old URL structure or a mistyped path.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that name a broken address as their main one
plainWhat: These pages name a main address that doesn't work (their "canonical" link leads to an error).
Search engines can't show an address that fails, so the instruction does nothing and they choose for themselves.
The cause is usually an out-of-date address, such as one from a test copy of the site.
plainFix: Open the main address the list shows for one of the pages in your browser, to see the error.
If your site's editor has a "canonical" box for the page, often under "SEO", put the page's own address in it.
If the same wrong address is on many pages, ask your developer to correct it in the page design.
checks.plainPassed: No page names a broken address as its main one
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

checks.title: Canonical points to a redirect
checks.description: The page's canonical names a URL that redirects. The detail gives the URL the redirects end at, or says that they lead back to this page. Where the crawl didn't check that URL, or was refused there, the detail says so: it is where the redirects lead, and may not be where they end.
checks.fix: Change the canonical to the redirect's final URL, which the detail gives; when the redirect leads back here, that's this page's own URL. If the detail says the URL wasn't checked, or was refused, open it first and use the address you end up at: it may redirect again.
checks.why: A canonical should name the final URL you want indexed. Naming a redirect sends search engines two signals that disagree: the canonical says to index the named URL, and its redirect says to index another. When the redirect leads back to this page, such as a canonical to /page on /page/ when /page redirects to /page/, this page most likely stays the indexed one, but the canonical is still wrong.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that name a forwarding address as their main one
plainWhat: These pages name a main address (a "canonical" link) that forwards visitors on to another address.
That gives search engines two answers to one question, and they may not pick the one you want.
Often it forwards straight back to the page itself, which does little harm but is still worth tidying.
plainFix: Look at where each main address in the list ends up: the list names the address, and says when it couldn't be checked.
Put that final address in the "canonical" box of your site's editor, often under "SEO", if it has one.
Ask your developer to correct it in the page design if the same thing shows on many pages.
checks.plainPassed: No page names a forwarding address as its main one
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

checks.title: Canonical points to a non-indexable page
checks.description: The page's canonical names another URL on the site that can't be indexed itself: it's noindex, canonicalised to yet another URL, or blocked by robots.txt. A URL that refused the crawler (a firewall, a bot challenge or a rate limit) isn't judged, as that says nothing about search engines; it's reported as blocked itself.
checks.fix: Point the canonical at the final, indexable URL. If the target isn't meant to be indexed, this page probably shouldn't name it as canonical.
checks.why: A canonical asks search engines to index the named URL instead of this one, so if that URL is noindex, blocked or points elsewhere in turn, the signals contradict each other and the outcome is up to Google. Google's own checklist includes making sure the canonical target isn't noindex. Canonical chains (A to B to C) usually come from content that moved more than once.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that name a main address search engines can't show
plainWhat: These pages name a main address (a "canonical" link) that can't itself appear in search results.
The page says "show that one instead", while that one says "don't show me", so the outcome is left to Google.
The list says what holds each one back, such as an instruction to stay out of search.
plainFix: Look at the main address the list shows for each page, and why it can't appear in search.
If that address should appear in search, ask your developer to remove what holds it back.
If it shouldn't, ask them to point the page's canonical link at its own address, or at one that can appear.
checks.plainPassed: No page names a main address that search can't show
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

checks.title: Canonical outside <head>
checks.description: The page's only canonical links are in the <body> as browsers parse it, and there's no canonical HTTP Link header.
checks.fix: Move the canonical into the <head>, as early as you can, and remove the element that ends the head early (or move it into the body).
checks.why:
Google only accepts rel="canonical" in the , so the page has no canonical in effect. Often the tag is in the head in the source, but an element that doesn't belong there, such as an , a
or stray text from a script or plugin, ends the head early and pushes everything after it into the body. The same break can push other head tags, such as hreflang, out too.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Main address written in the wrong part of the page
plainWhat: These pages name their main address (a "canonical" link) in a part of the page where search engines ignore it.
So the pages have no main address in effect, and Google chooses one itself.
It usually means something added near the top of the page's code, by a plugin or script, has pushed it out of place.
plainFix: Note any plugin, tracking code or banner added to the site lately, as one of them may be the cause.
Send the list to your developer: the canonical link must sit in the page's "head" section.
Ask them to move or remove whatever ends that section early.
checks.plainPassed: No main address is written in the wrong part of the page
checks.plainLooksFor: Main addresses written in the wrong part of the page

checks.title: Relative canonical URL
checks.description: The canonical in the HTML is a relative URL, such as /page or //example.com/page, instead of a full URL with https:// and the host.
checks.fix: Write the canonical as a full URL, such as https://www.example.com/page.
checks.why: Google supports relative canonicals, but recommends absolute URLs because relative ones can cause problems later, for example when a testing copy of the site gets crawled and its canonicals point at itself. A mistyped relative path (page instead of /page) also resolves against the current folder. Low priority if the canonicals resolve to the right URLs.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Main address written as a partial address
plainWhat: These pages give their main address in a short form, such as /page, without "https://" and your site's name.
Google can read the short form, but recommends the full address.
A short form can end up pointing at the wrong place, for example on a test copy of the site.
If your main addresses already lead to the right pages, there's nothing to do now.
plainFix: Send the list to your developer when they next work on the site: it isn't urgent.
Ask them to write each page's main address (its "canonical" link) in full, starting with "https://" and your site's name.
checks.plainPassed: No main address is written as a partial address
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly how your page design or SEO plugin writes the main address on every page.
checks.plainLooksFor: Main addresses written as partial addresses

checks.title: Invalid canonical URL
checks.description: A canonical in the <head> or an HTTP Link header has a value that isn't a valid http or https URL, such as an empty href, a template placeholder or a malformed address.
checks.fix: Fix the template so the canonical holds the page's absolute URL, or remove the broken tag.
checks.why: Search engines can't resolve it, so it's ignored: if it's the page's only canonical, the page has none in effect. It's usually a template variable that didn't fill in.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages whose main address isn't a real web address
plainWhat: These pages name a main address (a "canonical" link) that is empty or isn't a real web address.
Search engines ignore it, which can leave the page with no main address at all.
It's usually a gap in the page design that was never filled in.
plainFix: Look at what the list shows for each page: it says whether the address is empty or badly formed.
Send the list to your developer and ask them to make each page name its own full address, or remove the broken line.
checks.plainPassed: No page names a main address that isn't a real address
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a gap in your page design, which writes the same mistake on every page.

checks.title: Noindex page with a canonical to another URL
checks.description: The page is noindex and its canonical names a different URL, one that doesn't lead back to this page or to a broken URL.
checks.fix: If the page duplicates the other URL, remove the noindex and keep the canonical. If it should stay out of search, keep the noindex and make the canonical point to the page itself, or remove it.
checks.why: The two signals say different things: noindex asks for the page to be dropped from search, while the canonical says it's a duplicate whose signals belong to the other URL. Google hasn't documented which wins, and its guidance is to use rel="canonical", not noindex, to choose between duplicates on one site, since noindex removes the page from search entirely.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that give search engines two opposite instructions
plainWhat: These pages tell search engines to keep them out of search, and also name another page as their main version.
One instruction says "drop this page", the other says "treat it as a copy of that one", and Google doesn't say which wins.
Each page needs one or the other, not both.
plainFix: Decide, for each page, whether it's a copy of the page it names or a page that should simply stay out of search.
If it's a copy, ask your developer to remove the instruction to stay out of search (the "noindex").
If it should stay out of search, ask them to point its main address (its "canonical" link) at the page itself.
checks.plainPassed: No page gives search engines opposite instructions
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly one setting in your page design or SEO plugin, which names the same address on every page.

checks.title: Non-indexable URL in sitemap
checks.description: A sitemap lists this internal URL, but it can't be indexed as listed: it redirects, returns a 4xx or 5xx error, is blocked by robots.txt, is noindex or names another URL as canonical. URLs the crawler couldn't check, because of timeouts or firewall blocks, aren't included.
checks.fix: Remove the URL from the sitemap, or replace it with the final, indexable URL, such as the redirect target or the canonical. If the sitemap is generated, fix its filter rather than editing the file.
checks.why: A sitemap should list the URLs you want in search results, and Google treats every URL in it as a suggested canonical. Listing URLs that redirect, fail or ask not to be indexed contradicts your other signals and spends crawls on URLs that won't be indexed. It's usually a sitemap generator that doesn't filter by status, noindex or canonical.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Sitemap addresses that can't appear in search
plainWhat: Your sitemap, the file that lists your pages for search engines, includes addresses that can't appear in search.
Each one forwards elsewhere, fails, or is kept out of search some other way: the list says which.
A sitemap should hold only the addresses you want found, and these waste search engines' visits.
plainFix: Look at the reason the list gives for each address.
If the address should be found, fix that reason: it's often listed as a problem of its own.
If it shouldn't, take it out of the sitemap, or list the address it forwards to instead.
Ask your developer to change how the sitemap is built if your site makes it for you and has no setting for this.
checks.plainPassed: No sitemap lists an address that can't appear in search

checks.title: Indexable page not in a sitemap
checks.description: This indexable page isn't in any sitemap the crawl read. It's only checked when the crawl finished and every declared sitemap could be read.
checks.fix: Add the page to your XML sitemap, ideally by making sure the generator includes every indexable page type.
checks.why: Search engines can still find it through links, and on a small, well-linked site that's enough: Google says sites of about 500 pages or fewer that are comprehensively linked may not need a sitemap. On large or fast-changing sites, a complete sitemap helps new and updated pages get discovered sooner. Leaving out some page types, such as filtered or paginated listings, can be deliberate. Login, account and basket pages don't belong in a sitemap: they're better kept out of search with noindex.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages missing from your sitemap
plainWhat: These pages can appear in search, but aren't in your sitemap: the file that lists your pages for search engines.
Search engines can still find them through links, which is enough on a small site.
On a big or fast-changing site, a full sitemap helps new pages get found sooner.
Leaving pages out on purpose is fine, and login, basket and account pages are better kept out of search altogether.
plainFix: Look down the list for pages you want found quickly, such as new products or articles.
Find the sitemap options in your site's SEO settings or plugin, and include the kinds of page that are missing.
Ask your developer to add them if your sitemap is built another way.
checks.plainPassed: No page is missing from the sitemap

checks.title: Sitemap can't be read
checks.description: A sitemap listed in robots.txt, a sitemap index or the crawl settings returned an error (including 404), didn't respond, or isn't valid sitemap XML. Reported on the home page; the detail lists up to three, with their errors.
checks.fix: Open the sitemap URL to see the error, then fix the file or the server: it must be valid XML, at most 50 MB uncompressed and 50,000 URLs. If the sitemap no longer exists, remove its reference from robots.txt or the sitemap index.
checks.why: Search engines get no URLs from a sitemap they can't fetch or parse: Google keeps retrying for a few days, then stops trying that URL. Well-linked pages are still found, but what the sitemap adds, such as quicker discovery of new and deep pages, is lost. A referenced sitemap that returns 404 is usually stale and only needs removing.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: A sitemap on your site can't be read
plainWhat: A sitemap your site points search engines to can't be read: it's missing, fails to load, or has mistakes in it.
A sitemap is a file that lists your pages for search engines, and they get nothing from one they can't read.
Pages with links to them are still found, but new pages may take longer to show up in search.
plainFix: Open the sitemap's address from the list in your browser, to see the error.
If your site's SEO settings or plugin make the sitemap, use them to build it again.
If the sitemap no longer exists, ask your developer to remove the line that names it from your rules file (its "robots.txt").
Send the error to your developer otherwise: the file must load and be a valid sitemap of at most 50,000 addresses.
checks.plainPassed: No sitemap fails to load or has mistakes in it
checks.plainLooksFor: A sitemap that can't be read

checks.title: No XML sitemap found
checks.description: The crawl found no sitemap: none is listed in robots.txt or the crawl settings, and there's none at /sitemap.xml. Reported on the home page, only when sitemap discovery was on and the crawl finished.
checks.fix: Publish an XML sitemap of your indexable pages (most CMSs can generate one) and add a Sitemap: line with its full URL to robots.txt.
checks.why: A sitemap isn't required: Google finds pages through links, and a small, well-linked site may not need one. It helps most on large sites, new sites with few links from elsewhere, and sites with pages that links don't reach. A sitemap at another path that's only submitted in Search Console isn't visible to this crawl, so this may not be a real gap.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: No sitemap found
plainWhat: The check found no sitemap: a file that lists your pages for search engines.
A small site whose pages all link to each other can manage without one, as Google finds pages by following links.
It helps most on big or new sites.
If you gave your sitemap straight to Google, in Search Console, it won't show here, and there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Look in your site's SEO settings or plugin: most can create a sitemap with one switch.
Ask your developer to add its address to the site's rules file for search engines (its "robots.txt"), so they all find it.
Check the site again: it can then also find pages missing from your sitemap, and pages in it that nothing links to.
checks.plainPassed: A sitemap was found, or the site names one

checks.title: Sitemap lists a URL on another host
checks.description: A sitemap lists this URL, but it's on a different host from the sitemap: another site, or another of this site's hosts, such as www in a sitemap on the bare domain. The detail says how the URL answered.
checks.fix: List the URL as it is on the sitemap's own host now (usually where it redirects), or remove the entry. For a sitemap that deliberately covers several hosts, set up cross-submission through Search Console or robots.txt.
checks.why: The sitemaps protocol only accepts URLs on the sitemap's own host and drops the rest, so the page it was meant for isn't submitted. Google makes an exception for cross-submission: when every site involved is verified in Search Console and the sitemap is submitted there, or the other host's robots.txt references the sitemap. It's common after a move to or from www.
checks.subject: url
checks.plainTitle: Sitemap addresses outside its own website
plainWhat: Your sitemap lists addresses on another website, or on another version of your own, such as with or without "www".
Search engines drop those entries, so the pages they were meant for aren't put forward.
It's common after a site moves to or from "www".
plainFix: Compare the start of the addresses in the list with the start of your sitemap's own address.
Build the sitemap again from your site's SEO settings or plugin, so it lists each page at its current address.
Ask your developer to correct the web address your site is set to, if the sitemap keeps using the old one.
Take out any address that belongs to another website altogether.
checks.plainPassed: No sitemap lists an address outside its own website

checks.title: Missing title
checks.description: This indexable page has no <title> element, or its first one is empty.
checks.fix: Add a unique, descriptive <title> in the <head>. If a template sets it, check the field that fills it isn't empty for this page type.
checks.why: Google uses the <title> as one of its main sources for the page's title link in search results, and browsers show it in tabs and bookmarks. Without one, Google builds the title link from headings, anchor text and other text on the page, which may not say what you'd choose. Google asks for every page to have one, so fix this first.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with no title
plainWhat: These pages have no title: the text on the browser tab, and the link people click in search results.
Google has to make one up from other text on the page, which may not say what you'd choose.
Every page should have one, so fix these first.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and fill in its title, often under "SEO" or "Search engine listing".
Write a title that says what the page is about, and add your site's name if there's room.
If a whole kind of page has no title, ask your developer to set it in the page design.
checks.plainPassed: Every page has a title

checks.title: Multiple titles
checks.description: This indexable page has more than one <title> element (titles inside SVG images don't count). The detail says how many.
checks.fix: Keep a single <title> in the <head> and turn off the source of the others.
checks.why: HTML allows only one per page, and browsers use the first. Which one search engines use isn't documented, so the title you wrote may not be the one considered. A second title usually means two systems, such as a theme and an SEO plugin, are both writing the page's metadata.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with more than one title
plainWhat: These pages have more than one title in their code, where only one is allowed.
Browsers use the first, but search engines may use another, so the title you wrote may not be the one shown.
It usually means two parts of your site each write one, such as the page design and an SEO plugin.
plainFix: Check whether your site has two SEO plugins, or a page design with SEO settings of its own, both switched on.
Turn one of them off, so each page gets a single title.
If you can't find a second source, ask your developer what else adds a title to the page.
checks.plainPassed: No page has more than one title

checks.title: Title too long
checks.description: The page's title is longer than 60 characters (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings), counting full-width characters such as Chinese, Japanese and Korean, and emoji, as two.
checks.fix: Shorten the title or move the important words to the front; cut repeated words and long brand suffixes.
checks.why: Google sets no length limit for titles, but truncates title links to fit the device width, so the end of a long title may not show; 60 characters is a rough guide to what fits, not a rule. Google may also rewrite titles that are long-winded or stuffed with keywords. With the important words first, a cut-off rarely matters.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Titles that may be cut off in search results
plainWhat: These pages have a title of more than 60 characters.
Search results cut a long title off to fit the screen, so the last words may not show.
That's harmless when the important words come first, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its title.
Move the words that matter most to the front.
Cut repeated words and long endings, such as a slogan after your site's name.
checks.plainPassed: No title is likely to be cut off in search results

checks.title: Title too short
checks.description: The page's title is shorter than 30 characters (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings), counting full-width characters and emoji as two.
checks.fix: Describe the page in the title: add the specific topic, product or place and, if you like, the site name.
checks.why: Short isn't wrong: a brand or product name can be exactly right. But very short titles are often vague, such as "Home", "Products" or "Page 2", which Google's guidance warns against because they don't tell searchers what the page is or set it apart from similar pages.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Very short titles
plainWhat: These pages have a title of fewer than 30 characters.
Titles like "Login" or "Products" don't tell a searcher what the page is, or whose.
A short title can be exactly right, such as a product name, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its title.
Say what the page is about, and add your site's name if there's room.
Leave the titles that already say it all.
Skip pages nobody searches for, such as login and basket pages.
checks.plainPassed: No title is very short

checks.title: Duplicate title
checks.description: Another indexable page has the same title, ignoring case and spacing. The detail says how many other pages share it.
checks.fix: Give each page a title that says what's specific about it. If the pages really are the same, consolidate them with a redirect or canonical instead.
checks.why: Google asks for distinct titles on every page, because identical ones make it impossible for searchers to tell pages apart, and it may rewrite title links that repeat boilerplate. Duplicate titles often mean duplicate pages, or a template that leaves out the distinguishing detail, such as the product, place or page number.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that share the same title
plainWhat: Two or more pages have the same title: the text on the browser tab, and the link people click in search results.
Searchers can't tell the pages apart, and Google may make up a title of its own.
It often means two addresses show the same page, or the site's design leaves out what's different, such as the page number.
plainFix: Open each page in your site's editor and give it a title that says what's specific to it.
If two addresses show the same page, keep one and ask your developer to forward the other to it.
checks.plainPassed: No two pages share a title

checks.title: Missing meta description
checks.description: This indexable page has no meta description, or its first one is empty.
checks.fix: Write a one- or two-sentence summary specific to the page in <meta name="description" content="...">. On large sites, generate descriptions from each page's data, such as product name, price and key features.
checks.why: Google writes most snippets from the page's content, but uses the meta description when it describes the page better, and says high-quality descriptions can improve the quality and quantity of search traffic. Without one, the snippet is whatever text Google picks. Descriptions don't affect ranking, so prioritise important pages, such as the home page and key landing pages.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with no search description
plainWhat: These pages have no search description: the short text under a page's title in search results.
Without one (a "meta description"), Google picks some text from the page, which may not be what you'd choose.
It doesn't change where the page ranks, so start with the pages you most want people to click.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find the description box, often under "SEO" or "Search engine listing".
Write one or two sentences that say what the page offers.
Skip pages nobody searches for, such as login and basket pages.
checks.plainPassed: Every page has a search description

checks.title: Multiple meta descriptions
checks.description: This indexable page has more than one meta description. The detail says how many.
checks.fix: Keep a single meta description and turn off the other source.
checks.why: HTML allows only one per page, and which one search engines use isn't documented, so you can't be sure the one you wrote is the one considered for the snippet. It usually comes from a theme and an SEO plugin both adding one.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages with more than one search description
plainWhat: These pages have more than one search description in their code, where only one is allowed.
Search engines may read either one (each is a "meta description"), so the text you wrote may not be the one used.
It usually means two parts of your site each add one, such as the page design and an SEO plugin.
plainFix: Check whether your site has two SEO plugins, or a page design with SEO settings of its own, both switched on.
Turn one of them off, so each page gets a single description.
If you can't find a second source, ask your developer what else adds a description to the page.
checks.plainPassed: No page has more than one search description

checks.title: Meta description too long
checks.description: The page's meta description is longer than 155 characters (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings), counting full-width characters and emoji as two.
checks.fix: Put what matters in the first sentence and trim the rest, so the description still works if it's cut.
checks.why: There's no length limit, but Google truncates snippets to fit the device width, so the end of a long description may not show, and it often builds the snippet from page text anyway. With the key point first, the cut rarely matters.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Search descriptions that may be cut off
plainWhat: These pages have a search description, the text under their title in search results, of more than 155 characters.
Search results cut off the end of a long description (a "meta description").
That's harmless when the important words come first, so only pages where the cut loses the point need changing.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its description, often under "SEO".
Put what matters in the first sentence.
Trim the rest to about 155 characters, or leave it if the opening already works.
checks.plainPassed: No search description is likely to be cut off

checks.title: Meta description too short
checks.description: The page's meta description is shorter than 70 characters (the default, which can be changed in the analysis settings), counting full-width characters and emoji as two.
checks.fix: Expand it into a specific one- or two-sentence summary of what the page offers and for whom.
checks.why: There's no minimum, but a very short description rarely summarises the page, and Google uses the meta description only when it describes the page better than the page's own text. A short one is fine if it says everything that matters.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Very short search descriptions
plainWhat: These pages have a search description, the text under their title in search results, of fewer than 70 characters.
One that short (a "meta description") rarely says enough, so Google often shows text from the page instead.
A short one that says everything that matters is fine, and then there's nothing to do.
plainFix: Open the page in your site's editor and find its description, often under "SEO".
Write one or two sentences that say what the page offers, and who it's for.
checks.plainPassed: No search description is very short

checks.title: Duplicate meta description
checks.description: Another indexable page has the same meta description, ignoring case and spacing. The detail says how many other pages share it.
checks.fix: Write a page-specific description, or generate one from each page's own data.
checks.why: Google says identical descriptions aren't helpful when individual pages appear in search, and recommends a unique one per page, with site-level wording only on the home page and other aggregation pages. Repeated descriptions usually come from a template default.
checks.subject: page
checks.plainTitle: Pages that share the same search description
plainWhat: Two or more pages share one search description: the short text under a page's title in search results.
Searchers can't tell the pages apart, and Google tends to write its own text instead.
The shared text (a "meta description") often comes from a default that the site's design fills in.
plainFix: Open each page in your site's editor and find its description, often under "SEO" or "Search engine listing".
Write one or two sentences that say what's on that page and nowhere else.
Leave numbered pages of one list (page 2, page 3) until last: they matter least.
checks.plainPassed: No two pages share a search description
checks.plainOneFix: That's almost certainly a default description that your page design or SEO plugin gives to pages without one of their own.

checks.title: Missing H1
